Data inspection with `node -e`: src/data/forecast-method.json in full; src/data/forecast-cache.json (all 6,016 series x 21 days scanned for NaN/negative/inverted intervals); src/data/demand-district-daily.json metadata; src/data/national-snapshot.json; all 154 files in src/data/districts/ (scanned for non-finite numbers, nulls, and cover/lead/P(out) contradictions); src/data/federated/27.json.

Hand-verified the backtest calendar arithmetic end to end (artefact startDate 2026-04-03 / 180 days; contextFrom 62 = 2026-06-04, holdoutFrom 152 = 2026-09-02; Phase B sim indices 247/337 map onto artefact 62/152 through sliceFrom = 365-180 = 185).

Ran five read-only tsx probes from the scratchpad against the real modules (no repo file created or modified, no build, no test, no gcloud):
- probe1: sampler determinism across simulation counts, Croston and TimesFM paths.
- probe2: Monte-Carlo mean daily demand vs published risk.forecastDailyDemand, grouped by fit method x seasonality profile, over all 915 Lucknow positions.
- probe4: lead-time demand from the Monte Carlo and from forecastDailyDemand, both against the simulator's ACTUAL future demand (simulateInventory extended 21 days past as-of; verified the extension reproduces the history bit-for-bit).
- probe5/probe6: severity reclassification over Lucknow + Pune + Ernakulam (2,972 positions), split flat vs seasonal as a control.
- probe8: a deliberately malformed cache entry (truncated lo/hi) through computeStockRisk.
- probe9: the single contradictory shipped row quoted below.

findings.title: Croston-path Monte Carlo de-seasonalises the smooth class twice, so stock-out risk on seasonal drugs is computed against ~half the demand the same record publishes
findings.evidence:
risk.ts:150-156 builds the per-day demand parameters from the OCCURRENCE RATE and the CONDITIONAL SIZE:

  function crostonDayParams(fit: DemandFit, multipliers: number[]): DayParams[] {
    const p = fit.demandProbability;
    const scaleOccurrence = fit.pattern === 'intermittent' || fit.pattern === 'lumpy';
    return multipliers.map((mult) => {
      if (!scaleOccurrence) {
        return { p, sizeMean: fit.meanSize * mult, sizeSd: fit.sigmaSize * mult };

The multipliers come from relativeMultipliers (risk.ts:104-113), which divides the forward curve by the as-of month's index:

  const fitSeason = seasonalIndex(profile, asOf);
  ...
  return mult.map((m) => m / fitSeason);

Its docstring (risk.ts:75-85) justifies that division for ONE quantity only: "`fit.meanDemand` is an exponentially-weighted level with alpha = 0.15 ... lately already includes the current month's seasonality." But for the smooth class the method is `ses`, and croston.ts:200-202 sets

    meanDemand = ses(series, alpha);      // EWMA level -- seasonally current
    meanSize = meanSizeObs;               // ANNUAL mean of non-zero days
    probability = nonZeroPeriods / periods; // ANNUAL occurrence frequency

so p * meanSize is the ANNUAL mean, which was never seasonalised to the as-of month and must not be divided by it. computeStockRisk publishes forecastDailyDemand from fit.meanDemand (risk.ts:410) but draws stockoutProbability / reorderPoint / expectedShortfallUnits from crostonDayParams (risk.ts:432).

Measured (probe2, all 915 Lucknow positions, median of MonteCarlo mean daily demand / published risk.forecastDailyDemand):

  method/profile                      n   median ratio   sept index
  ses / flat                        246          0.996        1.000
  ses / monsoon_vector               12          0.483        1.935
  ses / summer_enteric               27          0.928        1.048
  ses / winter_respiratory           29          1.196        0.768

The ratio is 1/seasonalIndex(profile, asOf), exactly.

Ground truth (probe4: the simulator's own future demand over the lead time, simulateInventory extended past as-of):

  method/profile             n   MonteCarlo/truth   published/truth
  ses / flat               246              1.022             1.026
  ses / monsoon_vector      12              0.488             1.003
  ses / summer_enteric      27              0.964             1.095
  ses / winter_respiratory  29              1.272             1.011

forecastDailyDemand is right; the Monte Carlo is wrong. probe6 over Lucknow + Pune + Ernakulam (2,972 positions, flat drugs as a control group):

  positions: 2972  smooth/ses: 1021 (34.4%)
  flat      n=789  sev up 25  down 20  low/mod->high/crit 12 | leadtime demand vs truth: shipped 1.008  consistent 0.998
  seasonal  n=232  sev up 17  down  3  low/mod->high/crit 10 | leadtime demand vs truth: shipped 0.791  consistent 1.000
findings.failureScenario:
Lucknow district hospital, paracetamol (probe9, the shipped pipeline with no modification):

  {"facility":"DST-09-LUCKNOW-DH-001","drug":"PARA-500-TAB","seasonality":"monsoon_vector",
   "pattern":"smooth","method":"ses","source":"croston","onHand":3387,
   "forecastDailyDemand":534.17,"daysOfCover":6.3,"leadTimeDays":10,
   "stockoutProbability":0.0575,"reorderPoint":3426,"riskScore":4,"severity":"low",
   "impliedLeadTimeDemand":5342}

The same record says the shelf holds 6.3 days of cover against a 10-day lead time, that 3,387 units are below the 3,426 reorder point, and that the stock-out probability is 5.8% and the severity "low". Those cannot all be true. With the Monte Carlo drawing from the level forecastDailyDemand reports, it is 98% and "critical".

smooth is 34.4% of all positions (~27,900 of the 81,104 tracked nationally) and byPattern.smooth = "croston", so every one of them runs this path; ~23% of those carry a non-flat profile (~6,300 positions). 17 of 232 seasonal smooth positions in the 3-district sample change severity, 10 of them upward from low/moderate to high/critical. That propagates into national-snapshot.json totals.criticalPositions (4,683) and totals.highPositions (5,591) — both under-counted — into the alert board, and into the redistribution plan, which ranks receivers by expected shortfall. The suppression is worst on monsoon_vector drugs in September, which is the submission's own headline narrative.
findings.suggestedFix: Make the Monte Carlo's per-day mean agree with the mean the record publishes. In crostonDayParams, scale the conditional size so that p * sizeMean_d == fit.meanDemand * mult_d rather than fit.meanSize * mult_d — e.g. take `const base = p > 0 ? fit.meanDemand / p : 0;` and use `sizeMean: base * mult` with sigmaSize scaled by the same factor to preserve the CV. probe6 shows that construction gives 1.000 against the simulator's true lead-time demand for the seasonal smooth class (vs 0.791 shipped) and leaves flat drugs unchanged (0.998 vs 1.008). It also removes the separate SBA discrepancy below. Add an assertion to scripts/test-timesfm.mts or a new test that mean(leadTimeDemandSamples(...)) / leadDays agrees with risk.forecastDailyDemand to within Monte-Carlo error, for every fit method and every seasonality profile — that single invariant would have caught this.

findings.title: verify-guardrails.mts's "independent" audit redraws the planner's own sample vector bit-for-bit, so a sampler bug cannot fail it
findings.failureScenario: Change drawSize's gamma parameterisation in risk.ts so every demand size is systematically understated (say, swap shape and scale, or drop the Math.max(1, ...) clamp). The planner then computes donor stock-out probabilities that are too low and hands out stock it should have kept. verify-guardrails.mts recomputes P(out) from the identical understated vector, sees the identical too-low numbers, reports "0 breaches", and npm test goes green — the exact failure mode the comment at :57 says is impossible. The published claim "we never create a stock-out to fix one" would then be resting on a check that can only confirm the planner's own arithmetic, not the distribution underneath it.
findings.suggestedFix: Make the audit draw actually independent by perturbing the seed rather than the count — add an optional seedSalt parameter to leadTimeDemandSamples that is mixed into hashSeed (default '' so production is unchanged), and pass a distinct salt from verify-guardrails.mts. Then AUDIT_SIMS, the 1/AUDIT_SIMS tolerance and redistribute.ts's enforcementMargin all mean what their docstrings say. Until that lands, the three comments at verify-guardrails.mts:57, :178-179, :203-206 and redistribute.ts:266-270 overstate what the check provides and should be corrected.

findings.title: "AAROGYA_NO_BQ=1 ... Both paths are checked in npm test" is false — npm test never builds a snapshot and never sets the variable
findings.evidence:
DEFENSE.md:56-61 (the judge-facing document):

  **The batch completes and the console still renders.** `AAROGYA_NO_BQ=1` builds a
  valid national snapshot from censored Croston-SBA alone, with no network at all,
  and `npm test` builds it both ways.

README.md:90-91:

  ... and `AAROGYA_NO_BQ=1` builds a valid
  snapshot from censored Croston alone with no network at all. Both paths are checked in `npm test`.

src/lib/bq/client.ts:79-83:

   * `AAROGYA_NO_BQ=1` is the switch that proves the fallback works: the snapshot
   * build must produce a valid artefact with no network at all, using the
   * committed forecast cache and Croston. It is checked in the build, so the
   * fallback cannot quietly rot.

package.json "test" expands to 22 scripts: test:outline, test:forecast, test:resolve, test:capture, test:capture-rules, test:rate-limit, test:batch-bounds, test:cross-district, test:bq-series, test:timesfm, test:determinism, test:overlay, test:base64, test:alerts, test:census, test:dispatch, test:footfall, test:surge, test:markdown, test:federated, test:guardrails, test:claims. None of them is `snapshot`. `grep -rn "build-snapshot|run snapshot" scripts/*.mts scripts/*.mjs .claude/scripts/*.mjs package.json` returns only docstring cross-references plus package.json:23 ("snapshot": "tsx scripts/build-snapshot.mts"), which nothing invokes. .claude/scripts/verify.mjs:136 only READS the committed src/data/national-snapshot.json; its five steps are lint, tsc, npm test, npm run build, live/repo parity.

The closest thing that exists is scripts/test-determinism.mts:69-81, which builds ONE district (DST-10-PURNIA) twice with the cache off and twice with it on. It never sets AAROGYA_NO_BQ and never builds a national snapshot. scripts/test-bq-series.mts:258-263 sets the variable only to assert bigQueryEnabled() returns false, then restores it.

client.ts:80-81 also mis-describes the mode: "using the committed forecast cache and Croston". scripts/build-snapshot.mts:107 is `if (FORECASTS_DISABLED) return null;` — the cache is dropped entirely, as build-snapshot.mts:97 correctly says.
findings.failureScenario: A judge reads DEFENSE.md, asks "what if the Google AI call fails?", and is told the offline path is covered by the test suite. It is not: the offline snapshot build has no automated coverage at all. If build-snapshot.mts grows a dependency on FORECAST_CACHE being non-null — the block at :793-799 already dereferences it with ?? fallbacks, and any new field that forgets one would throw — the offline build breaks and nothing catches it. The check also cannot simply be added as claimed: an offline build writes seriesForecast: 0 / model: null into national-snapshot.json, and the very next step, test:claims (check-claims.mts:864), asserts the README says "**6,016** district x drug series" against that file, so the suite would fail on the step after.
findings.suggestedFix: Either add a real guard — a script that runs build-snapshot.mts with AAROGYA_NO_BQ=1 to a temp output path, asserts the artefact parses and that forecast.model === null and forecast.timesfmPositions === 0, and does not overwrite the committed snapshot — and wire it into npm test; or correct the three claims to say what is actually checked (that the Croston path is exercised per-district by test:determinism, and that the offline snapshot build is a manual check). Also fix src/lib/bq/client.ts:80-81, which describes AAROGYA_NO_BQ=1 as using the committed cache when build-snapshot.mts:107 drops it.

findings.title: The backtest's Croston comparator is not the mean path the risk engine simulates, so the per-class winner was decided on a model production does not run
findings.evidence:
docs/forecast-backtest.md:11 and scripts/backtest-forecast.mts:588 both publish:

  | comparator | Croston/SBA/TSB **as shipped** - `relativeMultipliers` and all, the same code the fallback path runs |

and backtest-forecast.mts:219-221 says "Croston exactly as production runs it". But both scoring loops use fit.meanDemand:

  backtest-forecast.mts:227   const eCr = fit.meanDemand * mult[d] - actual[d];
  backtest-forecast.mts:352   const eCr = m.fit.meanDemand * mult[d] - m.truth[d];   // Phase B, the deciding one

The shipped risk engine never uses fit.meanDemand for the distribution it draws from. src/lib/forecast/risk.ts:150-160 uses fit.demandProbability * fit.meanSize * mult[d], and those are different numbers:
  - sba (intermittent, erratic): croston.ts:110 sets meanDemand = raw * (1 - alpha/2), while p * meanSize = raw. The engine simulates 1/0.925 = 8.1% more than the backtest scored.
  - ses (smooth): meanDemand is the EWMA level, p * meanSize is the annual mean — the discrepancy quantified in the finding above.

Measured against the simulator's true lead-time demand (probe6, Lucknow + Pune + Ernakulam, smooth/ses positions on a seasonal profile, n=232): the backtested path lands at 1.000 of truth, the path the risk engine actually draws from lands at 0.791. probe2's per-method medians of MonteCarlo/published show the sba offset independently: sba/flat 1.098, sba/summer_enteric 1.085, sba/monsoon_vector 1.082 — the 1/(1-alpha/2) deflator, visible even where seasonality cannot contribute.
findings.failureScenario: forecast-method.json awards the smooth class to Croston on a Phase B margin of -1.3% (timesfmMase 0.7611 vs crostonMase 0.7711) — inside the 5% WIN_MARGIN, so it is a tie that goes to the incumbent. That 0.7711 was earned by fit.meanDemand * mult[d], a path 0.791/1.000 more accurate on seasonal smooth positions than the one the engine actually simulates. Had the comparator been the shipped simulation's own mean, Croston's MASE would have been worse and the smooth class — 26,789 of the 74,568 scored positions, and 34.4% of the network — could have gone to TimesFM instead. The published sentence "A demand class is served by TimesFM only if it beat Croston by more than 5% MASE on this holdout" is therefore resting on a comparator that is labelled "as shipped" but is not.
findings.suggestedFix: Score the Croston arm from the same construction the risk engine draws from, so the table measures the incumbent that actually ships (fixing the finding above collapses the two into one number and makes the "as shipped" label true). Until then, soften docs/forecast-backtest.md:11 and backtest-forecast.mts:588 to say the comparator is the published mean path (risk.forecastDailyDemand), not the Monte Carlo's, and re-run the backtest after the risk fix lands since the per-class winners may move.

findings.title: fitSeasonalIndex's shrink-toward-1 weight counts days, not years, so it saturates after a single month and provides no shrinkage at all on the data it is given
findings.evidence:
src/lib/forecast/seasonality.ts:86-91 states the purpose:

   * ... and shrinks it toward 1.0 in
   * proportion to how little data supports each month. Shrinkage matters: with
   * two Augusts of history you do not want to trust an August multiplier of 3.4.
   *
   * @param minObs months with fewer observations than this are pulled hard toward 1.

and :95 / :112-116 implement it as

    minObs = 30,
    ...
    const weight = Math.min(1, counts[i] / minObs);
    return weight * raw + (1 - weight) * 1;

`counts[i]` is the number of daily OBSERVATIONS in calendar month i, not the number of years. With daily data, one month of history gives counts = 28-31 and weight = 0.93-1.0, i.e. essentially no shrinkage; "two Augusts" gives 62 observations and weight = 1, i.e. exactly zero shrinkage — the opposite of the stated protection.

The only caller is src/lib/federated/node.ts:163-166, which passes the default minObs = 30 over daily series. The shipped artefact shows the effect: src/data/federated/27.json, item ACT-ASSP-ADULT —

  "index":[1.000547,1.000547,1.000547,0.487487,0.579776,0.806934,1.233824,1.384993,1.503703,1.000547,1.000547,1.000547]
  "monthObs":[0,0,0,28,31,30,31,31,29,0,0,0]

April's 0.487 comes from a single 28-day April with weight 0.93, and the 1.504 for September from one 29-day September. Also visible: the eight months with zero observations are set to 1 and then re-normalised over all 12, so they publish 1.000547 rather than a neutral 1 (harmless here at 0.05%, but it means "no data" is not exactly "no effect").
findings.failureScenario: A node joins the grid with 30 days of a single month — fitStateNode's own docstring at node.ts:72 calls out `fitDays = 30` as a supported case. Every observed month gets weight ~1.0, so its raw ratio-to-mean is published essentially unshrunk, which is precisely the "August multiplier of 3.4 from two Augusts" case the docstring says the shrinkage prevents. The damage is limited because pool.ts:76/140 drops any month whose indexSe is null and precision-weights the rest, and node.ts:204-214 publishes null for months with fewer than 7 contrast days — so the pool, not the shrinkage, is what actually stops a thin node being believed. The docstring credits the wrong mechanism.
findings.suggestedFix: Either make the weight count what the docstring describes — the number of distinct YEARS contributing to that month, e.g. weight = min(1, distinctYears[i] / minYears) with minYears around 3 — or correct seasonality.ts:88-89 to say the shrinkage is per-observation and that thin months are actually handled by indexSe and the pool's precision weighting. Separately, consider normalising over only the months that have observations so an unobserved month publishes exactly 1.

result.cleanAreas:
**The backtest holdout is genuinely held out.** I checked the index arithmetic end to end rather than trusting the assertion. demand-district-daily.json has startDate 2026-04-03, days 180, lastDate 2026-09-29, asOf 2026-09-30. Phase A's contextFrom = 180-28-90 = 62 (2026-06-04) and holdoutFrom = 152 (2026-09-02) are disjoint, and the length assertion at backtest-forecast.mts:151 is real. Phase B's simulator indices (SIM_HISTORY 365, holdStart 337, trainFrom 247) map exactly onto artefact indices 152 and 62 via sliceFrom = 365-180 = 185 in export-demand.mts, so the two phases score the same 28 calendar days. No holdout day reaches a context window, a share denominator, or a MASE scale: the fit, the uncensoredMean level and the trainTruth scale are all sliced to [0, holdStart). The AI.FORECAST horizon starts the day after the last context day, so the wire format cannot leak either.

**MASE/RMSSE denominators.** Taken from the training window only, and identically for both arms, so the non-seasonal-naive choice (documented at length at backtest-forecast.mts:29-40) cannot bias the comparison. Zero-denominator series are excluded and counted (seriesSkippedFlat, facilityPositionsSkipped) rather than given a 0 or an Infinity.

**The 5% win margin is applied exactly where it claims.** `winner: delta < -WIN_MARGIN ? 'timesfm' : 'croston'` on the Phase B facility x drug table, and forecast-method.json's byPattern matches those winners row for row: smooth -1.3% croston, intermittent -6.5% timesfm, erratic +1.4% croston, lumpy -4.2% croston. The gate is keyed on the facility fit's pattern in both the batch (pipeline.ts:211) and the live recompute (recompute.ts:141-144), so a committed report cannot move a row onto a different model than the one that scored it.

**The disaggregation does what the docstring says.** facilityShares normalises to exactly 1 (test-determinism.mts:99-110 asserts it to 1e-9), scaleForecast clamps the share at 0, and the all-zero district case spreads evenly instead of dividing by zero. The share window (last 90 days of uncensoredMean) is the same calendar window TimesFM read. The recompute path rebuilds the same carrier set with the same default seed 20260930 (facility-lookup.ts:37 vs facilities.ts:206), so districtShare agrees between batch and runtime.

**No NaN, Infinity or negative forecast reaches a shipped number.** I scanned all 6,016 x 21 cache values: no NaN, no negative means (decodeForecastRows clamps at 0). 54 (series, day) pairs have hi < lo and 644 have mean < lo, but all are at magnitudes <= 0.1 units/day on near-zero anti-venom series and intervalSigma's `Math.max(0, ...)` absorbs them. Scanning national-snapshot.json and all 154 district payloads for non-finite numbers returned 0; the only nulls are the intentional `escalateTo: null`. daysOfCover's Infinity is converted to the documented -1 sentinel at district-detail.ts:582.

**A truncated interval in the cache degrades safely.** I fed computeStockRisk a hand-built cache entry whose `m` is 21 long but whose `lo`/`hi` are 3 long — districtForecast accepts it (it only validates `m.length`), but forecastWindow's `arr[Math.min(i, arr.length - 1)]` clamp repeats the last bound instead of producing undefined, and the result was a finite, sane risk (P(out) 0.996, reorderPoint 77). Worth a note in districtForecast, but not a live defect.

**The TimesFM path itself is arithmetically sound.** forecastDayParams sets sizeMean = mean/p so p*E[Z] = mean exactly, guards p <= 0 and mean <= 0 before dividing, clamps the interval-implied variance at zero, and correctly does NOT apply the seasonal multipliers on top of a path that already learned them. probe2 shows the TimesFM positions carry none of the seasonal bias the Croston smooth class does. build-snapshot.mts:124-140 hard-fails on a cache whose forecastStart, horizon or confidenceLevel disagrees with the snapshot, so the z-table assumption in intervalSigma cannot silently drift.

**The offline snapshot is honest about itself, when it runs.** With AAROGYA_NO_BQ=1 the cache and the method map are both dropped (build-snapshot.mts:107, :157), every position falls back to Croston, and the snapshot writes model: null and timesfmPositions: 0 — the DEFENSE.md claim about `timesfmPositions: 0` is accurate by code reading. Only the claim that npm test exercises it is not (reported above).

REFUTED as filed. Three of the four load-bearing evidence claims do not survive an independent check, and the core exclusion is an explicitly documented decision at the exact line the reporter names as the gap.

WHAT IS TRUE (confirmed each):
- src/app/api/events/route.ts:65 does read `export const maxDuration = 3600;`.
- src/proxy.ts:69 `const METERED_PATHS = ['/api/ask', '/api/capture', '/api/commit', '/api/dispatch'];` and :79 `const METERED_METHODS = new Set(['POST', 'PUT', 'PATCH']);` — /api/events is absent and GET is never metered.
- Grep for maxConnections|activeStreams|MAX_STREAMS|openStreams|streamCount|concurrenc across src/ and scripts/ returns nothing. No connection cap exists.
- Live: `curl -D - .../api/events` returns `HTTP/1.1 200`, `content-type: text/event-stream; charset=utf-8`, no ratelimit-* headers.

WHAT IS WRONG:

1. THE ANCHOR LINE IS INERT, AND I MEASURED IT. The finding is anchored on `maxDuration = 3600` and its scenario asserts "the route keeps each alive up to 3600s". It does not. Next's own docs at node_modules/next/dist/docs/01-app/03-api-reference/03-file-conventions/02-route-segment-config/maxDuration.md say only: "Deployment platforms can use `maxDuration` from the Next.js build output to add specific execution limits." It is a build-output annotation, not runtime enforcement. `grep -rn maxDuration node_modules/next/dist/server/` (excluding sourcemaps) yields exactly two hits — `typescript/rules/config.js:108` (an editor tooltip) and `router-utils/typegen.js` (a type declaration). There is no request-killing timer in the standalone Node server, and Cloud Run runs a container, never reading Next's build output. Empirical confirmation: I held one live stream open and it closed at `ENDED after 122.651535s http=200` — ~2 minutes, not 60. The cited line does nothing on this deployment.

2. THE QUOTE IS MISATTRIBUTED. The reporter cites "Route comment lines 66-67: the SSE stream in particular must not be rate-limited". events/route.ts:66-67 are a blank line and `const HEARTBEAT_MS = 15_000;`. That sentence lives in a different file, src/proxy.ts:64-67.

3. THE "80 CONCURRENT" PREMISE IS UNSUPPORTED AND SELF-CONTRADICTING. The entire quantitative scenario rests on "README:681 deploy command sets no --concurrency, so Cloud Run's default of 80 applies." That same one-line command (README.md:681) also sets no --max-instances and no --min-instances — yet the reporter simultaneously cites README.md:690 for `min-instances=1, max-instances=1`. The snippet is demonstrably not the deployed configuration, so its silence on --concurrency proves nothing. The reporter treats the snippet's omission as evidence for one flag while a different line disproves it for another.

4. IT IS A DOCUMENTED DECISION, AT THE EXACT LINE CITED AS THE GAP. src/proxy.ts:64-67: "`/api/events` and `/api/overlay` are deliberately absent. Both are GETs, so `METERED_METHODS` already exempts them -- and the SSE stream in particular must not be rate-limited: it is one long-lived connection per open console, and counting it would disconnect the second tab a judge opens." The threat model is stated outright in src/lib/rate-limit.ts: "This is deliberately NOT authentication. It is a spend ceiling. The threat model is 'someone finds the URL and hammers it', not 'a determined attacker wants in'. Authentication would cost days and buy nothing on this rubric." The commit that introduced it is titled "Put a spend ceiling on the two public endpoints that cost money" (99083ce).

5. THE STATED MOTIVE MISREADS THE LIMITER. The scenario claims the attack defeats "the exact goal (keeping the live link alive until judging) that the rate limiter was built for." rate-limit.ts says the limiter protects the trial CREDIT — "the credit is what keeps the submission's live link alive" — i.e. a bill ceiling, not an availability guarantee. It never claimed to provide the latter.

6. /api/events IS NOT SPECIALLY EXPOSED. Every GET on the service is unmetered by design. I confirmed live that `GET /api/overlay` also returns 200 with no ratelimit-* headers. The root cause is architectural — one instance holding in-process state, no auth — and it is owned in four places: README.md:216, DEFENSE.md:161, DEFENSE.md:194 ("`--max-instances=1` during judging: the overlay and the ticket store are in-process"), SUBMISSION.md:84, plus "There is no authentication" in DEFENSE.md and SUBMISSION.md. Naming events/route.ts:65 as the location attributes a documented architectural constraint to a route.

I also checked and eliminated the one amplification angle that would have raised severity: the stream calls `await ensureRestored()` on open, but src/lib/durable/sink.ts:670-680 memoizes it on `globalThis`, so N concurrent connections trigger one BigQuery restore, not N.

WHY NOT "none": a genuine residue survives. There truly is no concurrent-stream cap, and the documented rationale at proxy.ts:64-67 argues against per-window REQUEST COUNTING ("counting it would disconnect the second tab a judge opens") — which would not rebut a concurrency cap of, say, 20, a different mitigation that was never weighed. SSE is also genuinely the cheapest way to pin a Cloud Run slot. So it is not zero.

WHY "low" AND NOT "high": the rubric reserves high for "a real defect a user or judge would hit". No judge hits this; it requires a deliberate adversary, which the project explicitly placed outside its threat model. It is not a wrong number, data loss, or a false claim. And the mitigation would not close the class anyway — an unauthenticated public service pinned to one instance is denial-of-serviceable by flooding any unmetered route. Reported as high/security; actually low.

(Adjacent, out of scope for this adjudication but noted since I was in the file: src/app/api/events/route.ts:173-175, `shutdown()` opens with `if (closed) return;`, so when `send()` has already set `closed = true` via the enqueue catch at line 104, a later abort returns before `clearInterval(poll)` / `clearInterval(beat)` at lines 176-177 — the 250 ms and 15 s timers then fire forever as no-ops. That is a separate latent timer leak, not the reported finding.)

9. curl'd /console (639,743 B identity, 90,898 B gzip) and all 10 JS chunks + CSS; extracted and analysed the 396,456 B inline RSC flight payload; grepped every snapshot field against the console client tree and gzipped a trimmed copy.

findings.title: simulateInventory calls Date.toISOString() once per simulated day: ~29 s of the 229 s build
findings.failureScenario: Every build. The 365 day-strings are identical for every position in a run: build-snapshot.mts pins ASOF (line 74) and historyDays defaults to 365 (pipeline.ts:105), and buildStates passes the same pair to every simulateInventory call. The LRU replay shows 156 buildDistrictState calls x ~634 positions avg = 98,904 position-sims x 365 days = 36.1 M toISOString() calls at 797 ns = 28.8 s of pure string formatting, recomputing the same 365 strings 98,904 times. That is 12.6% of the 228.6 s recorded in national-snapshot.json.
findings.suggestedFix: Hoist the day strings out of the per-position loop. A module-level Map keyed by `asOf.getTime() + ':' + historyDays` holding a `string[]` of the 365 ISO dates (and, for free, a parallel `number[]` of getUTCMonth values, which removes the second Date read at line 267). Then line 268 becomes `const today = DAYS[day];`. Roughly 8 lines; the strings are byte-identical so nothing downstream changes. Same pattern at src/lib/sim/resources.ts:99 and src/lib/sim/footfall.ts:200, though those loops are 180 days x 2,824 facilities and worth perhaps 2-3 s more.

findings.title: DONOR_GUARDRAILS.donorSimulations = 2000 is 79% of planner time; 1000 gives a byte-identical plan
findings.evidence:
src/lib/optimize/redistribute.ts:278
  donorSimulations: 2000,

Measured on the real Patna cluster (4,700 contexts, 47 drugs):
  one donor draw at 2000 sims = 1,099 us (940 draws in 1,033 ms)
  planner state held 2,093 distinct donor draws -> 2,093 x 1.099 ms = 2,301 ms
  plan with donorSimulations=2 (MC ~free) = 691 ms  <- the non-MC floor
  691 + 2,301 = 2,992 ms vs 2,932 ms measured at 2000. So 79% of planning is this draw.

Order-signature comparison (from>to:drug:qty:cost, sorted) at 2000 vs 1000 vs 500:
  DST-10-PATNA   2000: 2,932 ms 168 orders Rs93,160 | 1000: 1,555 ms identical=true | 500: 912 ms identical=false (167 orders, Rs93,100)
  DST-27-PUNE    2000: 1,510 ms  90 orders Rs44,539 | 1000:   895 ms identical=true | 500: 513 ms identical=false (88 orders)
  DST-08-BARMER  2000:   511 ms  18 orders Rs10,519 | 1000:   281 ms identical=true | 500: 162 ms identical=true
findings.failureScenario: Every build. state.donorSamples is a Map on nationalPlannerState that is never cleared for the whole 128-district run, so it also retains every draw: at 2000 samples its upper bound is 81,104 positions x 2000 x 8 B = 1.30 GB of packed doubles held live to the end of the build, which is GC pressure on top of the CPU. Halving to 1000 halves both. Across the run the donor MC is bounded at 81,104 x 1.099 ms = 89 s, and the measured draw rate (2,093 of 4,700 cluster contexts = 44.5%) puts the realistic figure near 50-60 s, so ~25-30 s of the 228.6 s build.
findings.suggestedFix: Change the one literal to 1000 and re-run `npm run test:guardrails` and `npm run test:claims` before trusting it. Two caveats I could not settle read-only: (a) the published per-order `donorStockoutAfter` field shifts by a fraction of a point even where the order set does not, so docs/guardrail-gate.json must be regenerated; (b) I confirmed identity on 3 clusters with a fresh planner state, not on the national run, whose shared state makes the plan order-dependent. Note also that `enforcementMargin: 0.005` (line 260) is already smaller than the standard error of the difference between two independent estimates at p=0.1 and n=2000 (sqrt(2*0.1*0.9/2000) = 0.0095), so 2000 is not buying the margin the docstring assumes it is. Do NOT go to 500 - it measurably changes the plan.

findings.title: computeStockRisk copies and fully sorts 600 samples to read a single quantile: ~7 s of the build
findings.failureScenario: Every build and every live recompute. The sort is O(n log n) with a JS comparator (~5,500 comparator calls per position at n=600) plus a 600-element copy, and 599 of the 600 resulting order statistics are discarded. 98,904 position-sims x 71 us = 7.0 s of the 228.6 s build, plus one throwaway 600-element array allocated per position.
findings.suggestedFix: Replace the sort with a quickselect (Hoare partition / nth_element) on a single copy, selecting index floor(q*(n-1)). Same value returned for the same input, O(n) expected instead of O(n log n), and it keeps `quantile`'s contract if you keep the helper and add a `selectQuantile(samples, q)` beside it. Measured headroom is the 83 ms -> ~15-20 ms per district, about 8 s over the run.

findings.title: Expiry-rescue pass recomputes a loop-invariant batch sort per (donor, candidate) pair
findings.evidence:
src/lib/optimize/redistribute.ts:1041-1044, inside `for (const cand of candidates)` which is itself inside `for (const donor of wasteDonors)`:
      const receiverEarliest = cand.ctx.batches
        .filter((b) => b.quantity > 0)
        .sort((a, b) => a.expiryDate.localeCompare(b.expiryDate))[0];

This depends only on `cand.ctx`. commitAllocation (line 372-377) mutates only the `committed` map, never `batch.quantity`, so no batch array changes during the pass - the result is invariant for the whole run.

Measured on the Patna cluster: 16,426 recomputations across 4,700 distinct contexts (3.5x redundant), 27.1 ms. The pass-2 candidate array construction beside it costs a further 83.2 ms per cluster.
findings.failureScenario: Every build, 128 times. ~19 ms per cluster of the 691 ms non-MC planner budget, about 2 s over the national run. Small, but it is pure recomputation: the same filter+sort+allocate runs once per donor that reaches this candidate rather than once per candidate.
findings.suggestedFix: Hoist it into a `Map<TransferContext, StockBatch | undefined>` computed lazily once per context, shared across the wasteDonors loop. While in the same loop, note `admissible(donor.facility, cand.ctx.facility)` is evaluated twice for every accepted rescue - once in the filter at line 1031 and again in the IIFE at line 1122 - so carrying the `Admissibility` object into the candidate record removes the second call for free.

findings.title: check-claims.mts parses the 21.4 MB district directory three separate times
findings.failureScenario: Every `npm run test:claims`, which is in the `npm test` chain and in the local gate. 64 MB of JSON parsed where 21.4 MB would do, for 216 ms. Genuinely minor in absolute terms - reported because the fix is mechanical and because it is the gate script that runs most often.
findings.suggestedFix: One pass that accumulates all four quantities (leadMin/leadMax, notPermitted, the economics roll-up, gateKm) into locals, or a single `const districtPayloads = readdirSync(districtDir).map(...)` hoisted above the first use. The three loops read disjoint fields of the same object, so nothing about the assertions changes.

result.cleanAreas:
Three of the brief's hypotheses I tested and found WRONG. Reporting them so nobody spends time on them:

1. roadDistanceKm is NOT a hot spot, and a distance matrix or spatial index would buy nothing. Measured on the real Patna cluster: pass 1 enumerates 44,454 (receiver, donor) pairs, of which 22,064 reach the haversine and 15,313 survive the range test. At ~0.1 us per haversine that is ~2 ms of a 2,932 ms plan. Across 128 clusters it is under half a second. The pair loop is also not quadratic in any dangerous sense: planForDrug is called per drug, so the real shape is 47 drugs x (7.6 receivers x 100 contexts), not 355 x 4,700.

2. The 2,000-element linear scans in stockoutProbabilityAt / expectedShortfall do not matter. Measured 1.444 us per scan over 2,000 samples (200,000 iterations); the upper bound of 15,313 in-range pairs per cluster gives 22 ms of a 2,932 ms plan. Sorting the samples once and binary-searching would save ~20 ms per cluster, ~2.5 s over the run, for a much larger change than the two above. Not worth it.

3. donorDistribution's memoisation IS keyed correctly. capKey(ctx) = facility.id + '|' + drug.id, and the sample vector is a pure function of (facilityId, drug.id, fit, leadTimeDays, asOf, forecast) - all constant for a given position, and statesFor is deterministic per district code so an LRU eviction and rebuild reproduces the same context. state.donorStockoutBefore is likewise computed once at ctx.risk.onHand, which does not change. Sharing nationalPlannerState across all 128 turns means each (facility, drug) is drawn at most once for the whole build, bounded at 81,104 draws. The expensive part is the sample count, not the key.

Also checked and clean:
- Repeated parsing of the big payloads in the BUILD (the brief's concern). forecast-cache.json (2.5 MB) is parsed exactly once per build, in loadForecastCache at build-snapshot.mts:111. demand-district-daily.json (4.4 MB) is not read by build-snapshot.mts at all. The only genuine triple-parse is in check-claims.mts and it costs 216 ms (reported as low).
- src/lib/overlay/runtime-forecast.ts statically importing the 2.5 MB forecast cache is correct, not a leak: it carries `import 'server-only'` at line 1 and is imported only by api/ask, api/commit and dispatch/service. I confirmed against the live bundles that no chunk served to /console contains it.
- The client bundle has no dead weight to cut. 717 KB raw / 223 KB gzipped across 10 chunks: 229 KB is react-dom, 100 KB is the india-outline MultiPolygon the map renders, the rest is app code. No markdown/chart/date library is shipped.
- localeCompare on ISO date strings (inventory.ts:337, redistribute.ts:350/1015/1043) looks like a classic waste but measured as noise: 15 ns vs 2 ns per comparison, and on the 2-3 element batch arrays actually used the sort overhead dominates completely (sort3 with localeCompare 49 ns, with lexical compare 53 ns). Leave it alone.
- The LRU at STATE_CACHE_SIZE=32 does its job. Replaying the real district order gives 531 statesFor calls, 375 hits, 156 misses - a 22% rebuild overhead over the ideal 128, which is a reasonable price for the documented memory bound. Raising it to 48 would recover some of that but the docstring at build-snapshot.mts:238-245 explicitly trades this against hundreds of MB, and that is a decision already made.
- planRideAlongs re-drawing the receiver's samples (redistribute.ts:1266-1274) is documented at line 1264 as costing time and not determinism, and I measured it at roughly 25,000 draws x 275 us = 7 s over the run. Real, but it is a documented trade-off and small next to the donor draw.

result.reasoning:
CONFIRMED. I tried to refute this and could not; it reproduces exactly, and I found the decisive evidence the reporter only inferred.

1. THE LINE SAYS WHAT IS QUOTED. C:/Users/samar/aarogya-grid/src/components/IndiaMap.tsx:45-48, read directly:
 * It also bought us very little. State mean risk spans 11.2 to 19.6 across the
 * whole country, rendered at 0.16 fill opacity, so the layer was visually an
 * undifferentiated wash. Every question it was supposed to answer is answered
 * better by the district bubbles, which carry real coordinates.

2. THE SHIPPED ARTEFACT DISAGREES. src/data/national-snapshot.json ships a states[] array with meanRiskScore precomputed. Sorted, it runs 6.900 (Andhra Pradesh) to 23.100 (Bihar) across 16 states. I re-derived it three independent ways from the 128 districts[] rows: population-weighted 6.89 -> 23.12; unweighted 6.93 -> 22.60; tracked-position-weighted 6.94 -> 23.07. All three reproduce the reporter's figures to the digit. No aggregation I could construct yields 11.2-19.6.

3. THE COMPARISON IS APPLES-TO-APPLES, not a units mismatch. Line 34 describes the removed layer as "shaded by population-weighted risk". The shipped states[].meanRiskScore is exactly the population-weighted mean rounded to 1dp (AP 6.900 vs 6.89, Bihar 23.100 vs 23.12, UP 19.300 vs 19.32, Jharkhand 17.000 vs 17.00 — whereas the unweighted mean diverges, e.g. Jharkhand 18.75). So states[].meanRiskScore is the correct artefact to check the sentence against, and it does not match.

4. NEW EVIDENCE — IT WAS CORRECT WHEN WRITTEN, SO THIS IS TRUE DRIFT, NOT A FABRICATION. `git log -L 45,48:src/components/IndiaMap.tsx` attributes the line to 073d3ea ("Remove pre-2011 state boundaries; report plan economics honestly", 23 Aug 2026), whose commit message repeats the claim verbatim. I checked out that commit's snapshot (`git show 073d3ea:src/data/national-snapshot.json`) and computed its states[].meanRiskScore: it spans exactly 11.2 (Jharkhand) to 19.6 (Uttar Pradesh). The number was properly derived from its shipped artefact at the time and went stale in the 12 Sep re-score, exactly as the reporter surmised. That is the project's own claim-drift failure mode, confirmed by construction rather than assumed.

5. WHY THE GUARD MISSES IT — the "what does check-claims NOT cover" question. scripts/check-claims.mts scopes itself in its own docstring to "Every number on a surface a judge reads -- the README, the deck", and its reads are all JSON artefacts (national-snapshot.json, warning-rule.json, federated-summary.json, docs/*.json, src/data/districts/*) plus one .ts file read only to count tool names via regex (src/lib/ai/grid-tools.ts:70). It never scans .tsx docstrings. So source-comment figures are structurally outside the guard — a real, if narrow, blind spot.

WHY SEVERITY STAYS AT "low" AND DOES NOT ESCALATE:
- It reaches no judge-facing surface. I grepped the repo for 11.2 and 19.6: the only hit for THIS claim is IndiaMap.tsx:45. The README.md:401 and DEFENSE.md:201 hits for "11.2" are the assistant's slowest measured question (11.2 s) — an unrelated and correct claim. Nothing renders or computes from the docstring figure; it is inert prose.
- The decision it supports is not undermined. The independent reason in the same block — the boundary file was pre-2011 vintage, no Telangana, states labelled "Orissa"/"Uttaranchal" — is untouched, correct, and by itself dispositive. The reporter concedes this, honestly.
- The described layer genuinely no longer exists: there is no 0.16 fill opacity left in the file (the only fillOpacity is 0.78/1 on district bubbles at line 1301), so the paragraph is a historical rationale and the surrounding clauses are past tense ("bought", "was").

WHY IT IS NOT "none": the verb in the middle clause is present tense — "spans", not "spanned" — and it points at a field (states[].meanRiskScore) that still ships and that any reviewer can check in ten seconds against a now-3.4x span. In a repo whose stated first guardrail is "never publish a figure that is not read from a re-run script or a shipped payload", a shipped source file carrying a figure that no longer matches its artefact is a genuine, if minor, instance of the exact defect class the project polices. It is a factual mismatch, not a style opinion. Fix is one word plus two numbers: "spanned 11.2 to 19.6 at the time" or a re-derived "6.9 to 23.1".

REFUTED. The reporter's quotes and arithmetic are all exact — I confirmed every one independently — but the "claim-drift" framing collapses once you check how this codebase uses the phrase "~630 positions", and the stated consequence is affirmatively false.

VERIFIED AS ACCURATE (the reporter did not fabricate anything):
- C:/Users/samar/aarogya-grid/src/lib/district-detail.ts:405 does read "one district all ~630 positions are present, so the tier filter has real".
- district-detail.ts:561-562 does read: const positions: PositionRow[] = states / .filter((s) => s.risk.severity === 'critical' || s.risk.severity === 'high').
- My own measurement over all 128 files in C:/Users/samar/aarogya-grid/src/data/districts/: positions median 62, mean 80.3, max 231; severities exclusively {critical: 4683, high: 5591}; DST-09-LUCKNOW.json holds 203 positions (94 critical + 109 high) against trackedPositions 915; sum trackedPositions 81,104 / 128 = 633.6. Every figure reproduces exactly.

WHY IT IS STILL REFUTED:

1) "~630 positions" is an established term of art in this repo meaning positions EVALUATED per district, not positions shipped — and the decisive counter-example is in the SAME FILE, 334 lines below the disputed line. src/lib/district-detail.ts:739: "* shipping all ~630 positions to compute one mean per node." There the phrase unambiguously denotes the full FacilityDrugState[] set (the `states` array being filtered at line 562) and is explicitly contrasted WITH shipping. Same usage at src/lib/snapshot-types.ts:9 ("Evaluating one district -- simulating a year of ledger for ~630 stock positions") and scripts/build-snapshot.mts:241 ("each district holds 365 days of ledger for ~630 positions"). Read the way the author uses it in all three other instances, line 405 asserts that the complete ~630-position set is in scope to filter FROM — the contrast being the national board, which samples two per (district, tier) BEFORE any filtering is possible. That reading is true. The reporter even derives the correct meaning ("it is the count of positions EVALUATED") but treats it as evidence of drift, when it is in fact the author's consistent usage.

2) Lines 398 and 405 are therefore complementary, not contradictory: 398 describes what the field CONTAINS ("Every critical and high position"), 405 describes what it was filtered FROM. The reporter's core rhetorical claim — "Two claims in one comment block that cannot both be true" — does not hold.

3) THE FAILURE SCENARIO CANNOT REPRODUCE. The reporter says a tier whose facilities are all healthy contributes zero rows, undermining "real rows behind every chip". src/components/DistrictConsole.tsx:564 forecloses this: {TIERS.filter((t) => (tierCounts[t.key] ?? 0) > 0).map((t) => ( — zero-count chips are never rendered. Empirically the guarantee also holds on the merits: tier totals across all 128 payloads are {DH: 1013, CHC: 1212, PHC: 4298, SC: 3751}, i.e. sub-centres are the second-largest tier — exactly the pathology ("228 district hospitals and zero sub-centres") the comment claims to have fixed. Only 1 of 128 districts (DST-28-GUNTUR, 24 positions, no DH) lacks a tier, and there the chip simply does not render. The reporter reasoned about the consumer without reading it.

4) NO SHIPPED NUMBER OR USER-VISIBLE SURFACE IS WRONG. DistrictConsole.tsx:169-170 labels the panel exactly "{count(visiblePositions.length)} of {count(detail.positions.length)} critical + high"; the empty states at :595 and :602 read "has no critical or high-severity position" and "No critical or high-severity positions match this filter." Nothing a judge reads misstates the payload. This is not the project's serious finding class (a number on a surface not matching its artefact) — it touches no surface at all.

RESIDUAL, AND WHY IT IS "none" NOT "low": in strict isolation the word "present" at :405 could be misread as "present in this array", and a reader could stumble for a beat. But line 398, seven lines above in the same block, resolves it immediately, and the phrase is used identically three other times in the codebase. An ambiguous-but-defensible word choice in a comment that the adjacent line disambiguates, with no code defect, no data defect and no surface impact, is a wording preference — which the audit brief explicitly excludes ("NO STYLE OPINIONS"). Severity: none. Medium was never defensible under this rubric, which reserves medium for a latent bug or a real inefficiency; the code, the data and the UI are all correct here.

NOT REFUTED — the code says what the reporter claims, and I confirmed the deployed configuration crosses the family boundary. But the severity is medium, not high.

WHAT I VERIFIED MYSELF (src/lib/ai/grid-agent.ts):
- 519-535: `const request = { model: opts.model, contents, config: { ... thinkingConfig: thinkingFor(activeModel), ... } }` is constructed once per TURN, outside the retry loop.
- 538-540: `for (let attempt = 0; ; attempt++) { try { response = await ai.models.generateContent({ ...request, model: activeModel }); ...` — a shallow spread, so `config` stays the identical object across attempts.
- 554-558: `if (isDailyQuota(e) && activeModel !== fallbackModel) { ...; stripThoughtSignatures(contents); activeModel = fallbackModel; continue; }` — only `activeModel` is reassigned; `request.config.thinkingConfig` is never recomputed before the `continue`.
- 102-118 `thinkingFor`: `if (/gemini-3/.test(model)) return { thinkingLevel: level };` else `return { thinkingBudget: budget };`. Docstring 94-97 quoted accurately ("Sending the wrong one is a 400, so the family is decided from the active model id").
- 425-427 `isDailyQuota(e)` = `e.message.includes('PerDay')`; 406-414 `rateLimitDelayMs` returns null unless `status === 429` or the message contains `RESOURCE_EXHAUSTED`; 562 `if (waitMs === null || attempt >= RATE_LIMIT_RETRIES) throw e;`. So a 400 INVALID_ARGUMENT on the fallback attempt is not retried — it propagates, and src/app/api/ask/route.ts:164-173 turns it into a generic 502 `upstream_failed`.

Walking it with concrete values: turn 0, activeModel='gemini-3.5-flash' -> config.thinkingConfig = {thinkingLevel: MINIMAL}. attempt 0 throws a PerDay quota error -> activeModel='gemini-2.5-flash' -> attempt 1 re-sends the SAME config, i.e. `thinkingLevel` to a 2.5 model. Deterministic; there is no path by which the retry gets a corrected config (only the NEXT turn's line 527 would, and there is no next turn if the attempt throws).

INDEPENDENT CONFIRMATION OF THE CONFIGURATION (not taken on trust):
- Live probe I ran: `POST https://aarogya-grid-215071922486.asia-south1.run.app/api/ask` returned `{"model":"gemini-3.5-flash","backend":"vertex","turns":2}`.
- src/lib/ai/client.ts:40 `export const DEFAULT_FAST_MODEL_FALLBACK = 'gemini-2.5-flash';` and client.ts:31-38 documents that asia-south1 serves exactly `gemini-3.5-flash` and `gemini-2.5-flash`, so `fastModelId()` is a 2.5 model either way. Primary 3.x + fallback 2.5 = the boundary is genuinely crossed, and `activeModel !== fallbackModel` at 554 is genuinely true.

CORROBORATION FOR THE 400 THAT DOES NOT RELY ON THE PROJECT'S OWN COMMENT:
- node_modules/@google/genai/dist/genai.d.ts:2769 — "Indicates the maximum thinking depth. Use with earlier models shall result in error."
- genai.d.ts:11449-11451 — thinkingBudget "(Gemini 2.5 only)"; "Starting from Gemini 3.5 models, the old thinking_budget will no longer be supported and will result in a user error if set."
Either way the code is internally inconsistent: it spends a 25-line docstring deciding the family-correct parameter, then ships it to the other family. And no test exists — there is no grid-agent test file at all; grep for `PerDay|fallbackModel|thinkingConfig` across test files returns nothing.

WHY MEDIUM AND NOT HIGH:
1. Reachability. The branch requires `e.message.includes('PerDay')`. That string is the AI Studio FREE-TIER quota id (`GenerateRequestsPerDayPerProjectPerModel-FreeTier`), which grid-agent.ts:421-424 itself names ("The free tier's daily allowance for a model"). The judged deployment reports `backend: vertex`, where quota exhaustion surfaces as per-minute/per-region metric messages, not `PerDay`. I could not construct a Vertex error containing `PerDay`, so on the surface a judge actually touches, this branch may never execute.
2. Delta, not cause. When the branch does fire, the run was already failing on an unrecoverable daily-quota error. Without the fallback branch the same error would take the `rateLimitDelayMs` path (429/RESOURCE_EXHAUSTED), back off once, and throw anyway. The bug removes a rescue; it does not create the outage. The reporter's line "the fallback ... is the thing that kills it" overstates this.
3. No published number is affected, no security or data issue, primary path untouched.

That is a genuine latent bug on an untested error path with a compound precondition — medium.

result.whatIActuallyDid:
Read `scripts/check-claims.mts` in full (1,466 lines, 121 claims) and ran it read-only (`npx tsx scripts/check-claims.mts`) — it reports "claims: 121 checked, all agree with the shipped artefacts", so every finding below is in the guard's blind spot.

findings.title: README's cold-chain upgrade figures contradict the shipped payloads: ₹40,065 claimed, ₹32,914 actually billed
findings.evidence:
README.md:119-121 — "The upgrade is now priced into the gate and billed to the order that causes it: of 325 cold-chain ride-alongs, **56 still clear the gate** at their true cost and pay **₹40,065** of upgrade between them, and the rest are declined."

Summed over all 128 shipped district payloads (5,578 orders, every one carrying a numeric `coldUpgradeInr`):
  { allOrders: 5578, rideAlong: 3008, coldOrders: 535, coldChain+rideAlong: 103, ordersWithUpgrade: 43, upgradeSum: 32914 }

Semantics confirmed in scripts/verify-cross-district.mts:167-174 — anchors never carry an upgrade (`filter((t) => !t.rideAlong).every((t) => t.coldUpgradeInr === 0)`) and "no trip is charged the cold-chain upgrade twice" — so ₹32,914 across 43 orders is the whole of what the plan bills. grep shows 40,065 exists nowhere else in the repo: only README.md:121.
findings.failureScenario: A judge reads "56 still clear the gate ... and pay ₹40,065 of upgrade between them", opens the district payloads the sentence is derived from (or asks the assistant, whose `list_dispatch_orders` tool surfaces `coldUpgradeInr` per order), and sums 43 orders paying ₹32,914. The rupee figure is overstated by ₹7,151 and the count by 13. Nothing in `npm test` catches it: check-claims has no claim mentioning cold-chain, 325, 56 or 40,065.
findings.suggestedFix: Re-derive all three numbers from the shipped payloads in a script that writes an artefact (or add a check-claims derivation summing `coldUpgradeInr` and counting `coldChain && rideAlong` over `src/data/districts/*.json`), then restate the sentence from it. On the current build that is 103 cold-chain ride-alongs, 43 paying ₹32,914.

findings.title: "59 rules that failed" / "60 candidate rules" is stale on four judge-facing surfaces; the artefact scores 80 and 78 fail
findings.evidence:
README.md:284-285 — "runs the real detector, and scores 60 candidate rules against 258 clean district-observations"
README.md:295 — "**23% precision is not a good number and it is published anyway**, next to the 59 rules that failed, in [docs/warning-tuning.md](docs/warning-tuning.md)."
README.md:563 — "npm run tune:warning   # inject surges, score 60 rules, publish the table"
SUBMISSION.md:88 — "published next to the 59 rules that failed."
DEFENSE.md:197-198 — "published next to the 59 rules that failed."
docs/pitch-deck.html:531-532 — "tuned against 126 injected surges and scored on 60 candidate rules" … "next to the 59 rules that failed"

The artefact the same sentence links to: `grep -c "^| k=" docs/warning-tuning.md` → 80 rows; `grep -c "pass\*\*"` → 2. `docs/warning-tuning.json` → `evaluations: 80`, and the doc itself says "Chosen from the 2 rules that clear the gate". 80 − 2 = 78 failed.

The grid in scripts/tune-warning.mts:325-326 and 585-586:
  for (const k of [1, 2, 3, 4, 5]) for (const e of [0, 0.1, 0.25, 0.5]) RULES.push({ k, e });
  for (const rule of RULES) for (const source of ['footfall', 'consumption', 'either', 'both'] as Source[])
= 20 × 4 = 80. The figures 60/59 are from when there were three sources.
findings.failureScenario: A judge reads "next to the 59 rules that failed" on the pitch deck, clicks through to docs/warning-tuning.md as the sentence invites, and finds an 80-row table with 2 passes. check-claims verifies the chosen rule, its four measured outcomes and that `tuning.scenarios.length >= 100`, but never asserts anything about `evaluations.length` — so `npm test` stays green while four surfaces publish a count that is wrong by 19.
findings.suggestedFix: Derive both counts in check-claims from `docs/warning-tuning.json` (`evaluations.length` and `evaluations.length − passing`) and update all four surfaces to 80 scored / 78 failed. It understates rather than flatters, which is why it survived.

findings.title: Deck's censoring table is unreproducible: the bias figures re-measure at −4.4%/−0.9%, and the "Error" column has no source in the repo
findings.evidence: docs/pitch-deck.html:499-500 — The raw ledger−3.8%18.4% Stock-outs excluded−1.0%15.5% under the header "And the fit is on corrected history | Bias | Error". docs/README.md:8-10 says exactly how this is meant to be reproduced: "Every figure on it is reproducible from the repository at a fixed seed: … npx tsx scripts/eval-censoring.mts # the forecast-bias figures". I ran it (read-only, 1.8 s, seeded `createRng(7)`, SAMPLE_PAIRS = 4000): OVERALL naive bias -4.4% | corrected bias -0.9% functioning -3.0% / -0.8% · strained -4.6% / -0.8% · disrupted -7.8% / -1.4% So the Bias column should read −4.4% and −0.9%, not −3.8% and −1.0%. The "Error" column has no producer at all: eval-censoring.mts:124 prints only ['district tier','pairs','stockout days/yr','unmet demand','naive bias','corrected bias'] and computes no error metric; 18.4 and 15.5 appear in no artefact, and `docs/forecast-backtest.md` (the slide's own footnote citation) carries no censoring table.
findings.failureScenario: A judge on the AI slide sees a four-cell table of measured model quality, follows docs/README.md's instruction to reproduce it, and gets different bias numbers and no error numbers at all. The script writes no artefact and is not in `npm test` (`eval:censoring` is a separate npm script), so nothing re-derives it and check-claims has no claim on it.
findings.suggestedFix: Make eval-censoring.mts write a JSON artefact, add a check-claims derivation against it, and either re-measure the Error column into existence or drop it from the slide.

findings.title: README says "Ten tools are exposed" and lists ten; the code registers twelve and exposes eleven by default
findings.evidence: README.md:446-449 — "Ten tools are exposed, all pure functions over already-computed data: `resolve_district`, `national_overview`, `district_status`, `facility_snapshot`, `list_positions`, `list_dispatch_orders`, `cross_district_flows`, `explain_forecast`, `explain_unmet_need` and `drug_reference`." src/lib/ai/grid-tools.ts declares twelve (grep "^ name: '"): resolve_district, national_overview, district_status, list_positions, list_dispatch_orders, cross_district_flows, explain_unmet_need, facility_snapshot, explain_forecast, drug_reference, early_warnings (line 1353), simulate_outbreak (line 1442). Only `simulate_outbreak` is `tier: 'on_request'` (line 1443), and `availableTools()` (line 1624) filters on that alone — so eleven are in front of the model by default. `early_warnings` is default-exposed and missing from the README's list. The guard derives the count correctly (check-claims.mts:70, toolCount = 12), publishes it on the deck (`12 tools`), and DEFENSE.md:23 says "twelve tools" — but the mustNot guard that would catch this is scoped to the deck only: check-claims.mts:1015 — { file: 'docs/pitch-deck.html', mustNot: /Nine tools|Ten tools/i, why: 'there are ' + toolCount + ' tools' }
findings.failureScenario: A judge reads "Ten tools are exposed" in the README, then "12 tools" on the deck and "twelve tools" in DEFENSE.md, and has to decide which document to believe about the AI surface — on a submission whose pitch is that no figure is typed by hand. The guard already knows the answer and already forbids this exact string, one file away.
findings.suggestedFix: Extend check-claims.mts:1015 to README.md (or better, assert `toolWord + ' tools are exposed'`), and update the README to eleven default-exposed tools of twelve registered, adding `early_warnings` to the list.

findings.title: The same measurement is published as 326 ms and as 178 ms, both attributed to the live deployment, with no artefact to adjudicate
findings.evidence:
README.md:18-19 — "the real-time loop closes through Cloud Run's load balancer — **two open tabs updated 326 ms after a commit**, `X-Accel-Buffering: no` set, first SSE frame flushed immediately (`npm run rehearse:live <url>`)."
SUBMISSION.md:60 — "server re-score in 7–14 ms → both open tabs updated in 326 ms"
README.md:185-187 — "Measured end to end by `npm run rehearse:live`, in a real browser, **against the live Cloud Run deployment**: **server-side re-score 11 ms** (budget 100 ms) and **178 ms to reach two open tabs** (budget 2 s)."
docs/pitch-deck.html:412 — "Measured against the live Cloud Run deployment: re-score 11 ms (budget 100) · two open tabs updated in 178 ms (budget 2 s)"

Unlike every other rehearsal, `scripts/rehearse-live.mjs` writes no artefact — `grep -n "writeFile\|docs/" scripts/rehearse-live.mjs` returns nothing; the figure exists only in console output (line 180: `ok('both tabs showed the new number in ' + delta + ' ms ...')`). findings.failureScenario: A judge reads 326 ms in the README's opening block and on the submission page, then 178 ms in the README's own §4b and in the deck footnote — four statements of one measurement, all credited to the live Cloud Run deployment, differing by 83%. findings.title: README says Kerala's worst district ranks 35th of 128; by the ranking the product actually uses it is 32nd

README.md:507-510 — "**District risk rankings are no longer arbitrary.** … The worst eight districts are now in Jharkhand, Bihar and Uttar Pradesh, and Kerala's worst district ranks 35th of 128 — because the anchoring indicator says so, not because we decided it should."

The product ranks districts by `meanRiskScore` descending — src/components/NationalConsole.tsx:86: `[...snapshot.districts].sort((a, b) => b.meanRiskScore - a.meanRiskScore).slice(0, 12)` (and IndiaMap.tsx:143, 517 colour by the same field). Applying that to all 128 districts in national-snapshot.json puts Kerala's worst (Idukki, meanRiskScore 15.6) at rank 32, not 35. findings.title: Deck says 37.21 Cr in catchment; the artefact and the live site both say 37.22 Cr
findings.evidence:
docs/pitch-deck.html:367 —
37.21 Cr
people in catchment
`national-snapshot.json` totals.populationCovered = 372164015 → 37.2164 Cr, which rounds to 37.22. The product's own formatter rounds rather than truncates for this field — src/lib/format.ts:63-67: `export function population(value: number) { if (value >= 1_00_00_000) return (value / 1_00_00_000).toFixed(2) + ' Cr'; … }` — and page.tsx:205 renders `population(f.populationCovered)`. The live site confirms: `curl .../ | grep -c '37.22 Cr'` → 1, and `curl .../console | grep -c '37.22'` → 1. (Note this is not the codebase's documented truncation rule: `truncateTo` in format.ts:44-54 is used by `compact()`, not by `population()`, so the deck is not following a deliberate convention here.)
findings.failureScenario: A judge with the deck open beside the live site sees 37.21 Cr on slide 2 and 37.22 Cr in the console's KPI strip — a 100,000-person disagreement between the two surfaces in the same field of view. Unguarded: populationCovered appears in no check-claims claim.
findings.suggestedFix: Add a check-claims claim on `population(t.populationCovered) + ' Cr'` for docs/pitch-deck.html and correct the slide to 37.22 Cr.

findings.title: docs/forecast-runtime.md says a full refresh is 4 batches; every surface says three statements and the code caps at three
findings.evidence:
docs/forecast-runtime.md:38 — "**A full refresh of all 6,016 series is 4 batches, ≈ 224–295 s run back to back** at the measured rate, against a 180 s budget."

Every judge-facing surface says three, and the production code agrees:
DEFENSE.md:154-156 — "All **6,016** district × drug series forecast in **three BigQuery statements** … → `docs/forecast-runtime.md`"
docs/pitch-deck.html slide 6 — "through BigQuery AI.FORECAST — three statements, 0 bytes billed, none declined"
docs/demo-script.md:26 — "three statements, zero bytes billed"
scripts/forecast-refresh.mts:54,106 — `const MAX_QUERIES = 3;` … `const perBatch = Math.ceil(wire.length / MAX_QUERIES);` → ceil(6016/3) = 2006 series × 3 statements, and line 122 refuses to run if it exceeds three.

The "4 batches" is scripts/forecast-ladder.mts:383 extrapolating from the ladder's top rung (`Math.ceil(o.seriesPool / top.requestedSeries)` = ceil(6016/2000)), not from the production path.
findings.failureScenario: A judge follows DEFENSE.md's "three BigQuery statements → docs/forecast-runtime.md" citation and the cited artefact says four. Harmless technically (the ladder is measuring a different batch size), but it is a citation that does not support the claim it is offered for.
findings.suggestedFix: Have forecast-ladder.mts compute the refresh batch count from `MAX_QUERIES` in the refresh path rather than from the top rung, or add a sentence in the doc distinguishing the ladder rung from the production batch size.

findings.title: check-claims contains a hard-coded '29' claim whose stated reason does not match what it checks, duplicating a derived claim

findings.title: Four guard claims match strings too short to prove what they claim; one already matches two different sentences
findings.evidence: Instrumented copy of the guard, printing each matched string's length and occurrence count. The shortest claims: len 7 "**23%**" (line 774, why: 'precision, published rather than buried') len 8 "**3.0%**" (line 543, why: 'the worst post-donation donor risk the audit found') len 9 "**≤ 10%**" (line 524) len 9 "**0.395**" (line 769, why: 'false alarms per district-week') len 9 "**5,578**" (line 800, why: 'dispatch orders') — occurs TWICE in README.md The `**5,578**` case is the documented failure mode already happening in miniature: the claim's stated purpose is the dispatch-order sentence at README.md:111 ("turn 2,798 orders into **5,578** on **2,078 vehicle trips**"), but README.md:170 ("the plan carries **5,578** orders rather than 7,097") satisfies it equally, so deleting the intended sentence would not turn the claim red. The file next door states the correct standard, having been bitten by it — .claude/scripts/verify.mjs:156-159: "A parity check that passes by coincidence is worse than no parity check, because it is believed. So the list is longer, every entry must be present, and it leans on values that cannot collide by accident." (That file's own `want` list still includes `['districts', 128]`, a bare three-digit substring searched in a 660 KB HTML document, which cannot fail.) Verified fix status for the incident the header docstring describes (the deck's "778 tablets / ×781"): that one IS properly fixed — lines 1019-1063 pin quantity, distance, both costs and both pick-list lines as long anchored strings ('spare 110', 'pick list: B010-DH001 × 12 (exp 2027-10-28)'). No claim currently produces a false PASS. The weakness is latent, not live.
findings.failureScenario: If the precision row is moved out of the table at README.md:293 while the prose at line 295 is edited to bold "**23%**", the guard keeps passing while the published precision is gone; likewise `**3.0%**` and `**0.395**` are single bold tokens that any future edit could satisfy accidentally. None of these currently mis-passes — I checked all 121 — but four of them assert only "this number appears in bold somewhere in a 723-line file".
findings.suggestedFix: Anchor them to their table rows the way the detection-rate claim already is ('| **100%** |' at line 758): e.g. '| Precision | **23%** |', '| False alarms per district-week | **0.395** |', and 'worst post-donation stock-out risk **3.0%**'. For `**5,578**`, use '**5,578** on **2,078 vehicle trips**'.

result.cleanAreas:
COVERAGE, MEASURED
232 distinct numeric tokens across the six primary judge-facing surfaces (README 272 raw / SUBMISSION 42 / DEFENSE 58 / NOTICE 25 / demo-script 89 / deck visible text 192; deduped to 232). check-claims makes 121 claims — 79 on README.md, 24 on docs/pitch-deck.html, 8 on DEFENSE.md, 7 on SUBMISSION.md, 2 on source files, 2 on JSON gates — plus 12 restart-gate bounds, 8 dispatch-gate rows, 11 warning-rule rows and 1 build-band assertion checked separately. Several claims pin more than one number (the "four zeros" claim pins four; the guardrail-cost claims pin two each), so the 121 claims pin roughly 130 distinct numbers: **about 56% coverage of the numbers a judge can read.** Zero claims touch NOTICE or docs/demo-script.md (114 numeric tokens between them) or any generated doc under docs/ other than guardrail-gate.json and assistant-latency.json.

I ran the guard read-only: "claims: 121 checked, all agree with the shipped artefacts." Everything it covers is genuinely correct — I spot-verified the derivations rather than trusting the PASS lines.

VERIFIED CORRECT AND GENUINELY SOUND (checked, not assumed)
- Live/repo parity is exact. curl against /console found all of 2,824 · 81,104 · 4,683 · 5,578 · 2,078 · 1,579 · 5,42,644 · 174 · 128 · 37.22 Cr · ₹1.92 Cr; /api/federated returns kind aarogya.federated.prior/1, 16 nodes, shared.numbers 25,184, the four zeros, rowsRetainedInStates 1,082,880 — byte-for-byte with src/data/federated-summary.json. Root cold-loads in 0.46 s against SUBMISSION's "well inside three seconds".
- The scaling section, which is the least guarded and which I most expected to have drifted, is exact. I re-derived the clustering from src/lib/domain/geo.ts at NEIGHBOUR_RADIUS_KM=250 / MAX_NEIGHBOURS=4: 78 of 128 clusters cross a state line (README: "78 of the 128 clusters"), greedy colouring gives 9 rounds with the largest at 31 (README and DEFENSE: "9 concurrent rounds (largest 31 districts)"), and replaying the LRU in build-snapshot.mts (STATE_CACHE_SIZE=32) gives 156 misses and 71% reuse (README: "156 district states are simulated rather than 128", "71% reuse on the 128-district run"). Four unguarded numbers, four exact matches.
- The census cross-check holds: worst divergence among the ten unchanged districts is 0.1447% → README's "0.14%" is right (the script's own docstring says 0.15%, but that is an internal comment). Bastar 578,326 vs undivided 1,413,199, Pune 48 facilities, Adilabad 12 — all exact. The worst eight districts by meanRiskScore are indeed all in Jharkhand, Bihar and Uttar Pradesh.
- README's "27 assertions" for test-resolve is right and I nearly reported it wrong: CASES has 25 entries, plus two formulary assertions at lines 106-125 = 27. test-capture's "26 assertions" = 26 check() calls. Five poisoned copies in verify-federated.mts POISON = 5.
- The forecast/backtest block is clean: 6,016 series, 21-day horizon, 90-day context, 28-day holdout, 5% win margin, intermittent won by 6.5%, 30,535 of 81,104 — all match forecast-method.json, and the deck's per-class MASE table (24,187/0.896/0.958 etc.) matches docs/forecast-backtest.md row for row. DEFENSE's "three BigQuery statements" matches MAX_QUERIES=3 in forecast-refresh.mts. Anomaly scale 6,144 series in 7 statements = 128+6,016 series and 1+6 batches in anomaly-runtime.json; "flagged 90 of 128 districts on footfall" exact.
- The economics are clean: ₹29.8 L / ₹70.9 L / ₹26.0 L / ₹3.8 L / ₹4.79 / 5,42,644 / 10% uplift over the 495,166 baseline all re-derive from totals. CONFIRMED by direct reproduction, with one correction to the reporter's trigger narrative and one respect in which it is worse than reported.

CODE VERIFIED AS QUOTED (src/app/api/events/route.ts): :83 `await ensureRestored();` is the first statement of GET; :96 the underlying source declares `start(controller)` and NO `cancel()`; :142 `poll` and :166 `beat`; :173-183 `shutdown` clears both; :185 `request.signal.addEventListener('abort', shutdown)` is its ONLY reachable trigger, registered after the await.

NEXT.JS 16.3.2 WIRING VERIFIED (node_modules/next/dist/server/):
- web/spec-extension/adapters/next-request.js:44 — `response.once('close', () => { if (response.writableFinished) return; controller.abort(new ResponseAborted()); })`. Client disconnect aborts the signal.
- next-request.js:104 — signal passed straight into `new NextRequest(url, {..., signal, ...})`; with dynamic='force-dynamic' the handler gets the unproxied request (route-modules/app-route/module.js:589 `request = req`).
- route-modules/app-route/module.js:462 — `res = await workUnitAsyncStorage.run(requestStore, handler, request, handlerContext)`. Handler is plainly awaited; no race against abort.
- ReadableStream `start()` runs synchronously in the constructor, hence after the await resumed, on an already-aborted signal. Per DOM spec the listener never fires.

REPRODUCTION (real HTTP server, signalFromNodeResponse copied verbatim, client destroys socket mid-await):
  start() entered. request.signal.aborted = true
  pipeToNodeResponse: EARLY RETURN, stream never read or cancelled
  shutdown() ran: false | intervals still live: 2 | (2s later) poll ticks: 19, queued bytes: 241 <- still climbing
CONTROL (disconnect AFTER stream is live): shutdown() ran: true, intervals still live: 0. So this is specifically the await-window defect, not a general cleanup failure.

WORSE THAN REPORTED: pipe-readable.js:120 `const { errored, destroyed } = res; if (errored || destroyed) return;` — when the socket is already dead the body is never read AND never cancelled. So enqueue never throws, `closed` never flips, and the full poll body (eventsSince/durabilitySince/ticketsSince) runs 4x/sec forever into an unread queue. The reporter offered this as one of two branches; it is the one that actually occurs.

LIVE PREMISES HOLD: GET /api/overlay returns restore.elapsedMs=1032, ticketRestore.elapsedMs=968, at=2026-09-12T19:58:54.697Z, instance aarogya-grid-00021-gjw-wm93mo. README.md:690 documents min-instances=1, max-instances=1, so an orphan lives for the container's multi-day life.

REPORTER IS WRONG ON THE TRIGGER: "judge opens /console; useGridEvents seeds and then constructs the EventSource; the GET blocks in ensureRestored()" does not happen. src/lib/hooks/useGridEvents.ts:230 is `void seed().then(subscribe);` — /api/overlay is fetched first and pays the cold start. By the time the EventSource opens, ensureRestored() returns an already-resolved promise, and awaiting a resolved promise yields only a microtask, which no I/O macrotask can interleave. A fresh /console load on a cold container CANNOT trigger this. The real trigger is the deploy path: an open tab's EventSource drops on a revision change and the browser's native reconnect re-issues /api/events DIRECTLY (useGridEvents.ts:190 handles 'error' by only setting state; only a server-sent 'refetch' calls seed()). That reconnect is the first request to touch the cold restore and blocks the full ~1s; a reload, navigation, or the hook's unmount cleanup (:232 `cancelled = true; source?.close()`) inside that second orphans the timers.

SEVERITY medium, as reported. Limiter: ensureRestored() memoizes on globalThis, so the vulnerable window is ~1 second PER CONTAINER LIFETIME, not per connection. Max orphans per deploy is bounded by the /api/events requests that both begin and abort inside that one second — realistically 0 to a few. Each costs 2 timers, cheap in-memory array work at 4 Hz, and ~14 bytes/15s of heartbeat into an unread queue (~115 KB/day). No judge-visible symptom, no wrong number, no security or data issue, so not high/critical. But the only cleanup path is provably unreachable in a reachable state and the leak has unbounded lifetime, so not low. Two-line fix: bail at the top of start() if request.signal.aborted, and add cancel() to the underlying source (which also covers the pipeTo-abort branch when res is closing rather than already destroyed).

UNVERIFIED, NON-LOAD-BEARING: that Cloud Run propagates client disconnects to the container (untestable without deploying, which was forbidden). If it does, the finding stands as described; if it does not, shutdown never runs for ANY connection, a larger bug. Either way not refuted.

Two corrections to the reporter's framing, neither of which saves the claim. (1) The deployed service does not carry the phrase — curl of the live landing page yields only "TimesFM 2.0 through BigQuery" — so the defect is confined to SUBMISSION.md, README.md, docs/pitch-deck.html and the derived docs/pitch-deck.pdf.
